theory.intro: Two rectangles can have the **same area** but **different perimeters**. A long, thin rectangle has a larger perimeter than a more square one of equal area.
facts: For a fixed area, the closer the rectangle is to a **square**, the **smaller** its perimeter.
steps: Find the area of each rectangle (should match).
Find the perimeter of each rectangle.

foundation.solution_text:
$P_A=2\times(8+3)$
$=22\text{ cm}$
$P_B=2\times(6+4)$
$=20\text{ cm}$
Rectangle $B$ has the smaller perimeter by $2\text{ cm}$.

foundation.question_text: List every different rectangle with whole-number side lengths and area $24\text{ cm}^2$. Treat a turned rectangle as the same rectangle. Give each perimeter.
foundation.solution_text:
$1\times24:\quad P=2\times(1+24)=50\text{ cm}$
$2\times12:\quad P=2\times(2+12)=28\text{ cm}$
$3\times8:\quad P=2\times(3+8)=22\text{ cm}$
$4\times6:\quad P=2\times(4+6)=20\text{ cm}$
There are $4$ different rectangles.

foundation.question_text: Rectangles with dimensions $1\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ all have the same area. Order them from smallest to largest perimeter.
foundation.solution_text:
$P_{1\times16}=2\times(1+16)=34\text{ cm}$
$P_{2\times8}=2\times(2+8)=20\text{ cm}$
$P_{4\times4}=2\times(4+4)=16\text{ cm}$
Smallest to largest: $4\times4$, $2\times8$, $1\times16$.

development.question_text: Find every rectangle with whole-number side lengths and area $36\text{ cm}^2$. What is the difference between the greatest and least perimeters?
development.solution_text:
$1\times36: P=74\text{ cm}$
$2\times18: P=40\text{ cm}$
$3\times12: P=30\text{ cm}$
$4\times9: P=26\text{ cm}$

$74-24=50\text{ cm}$

development.question_text: How many different rectangles with whole-number side lengths can be made with area $60\text{ m}^2$? Treat a turned rectangle as the same rectangle.

development.solution_text:
$72=1\times72=2\times36=3\times24=4\times18=6\times12=8\times9$
The factors $8$ and $9$ are closest together, so this rectangle is closest to a square.
$P=2\times(8+9)=34\text{ m}$, the smallest perimeter.

development.question_text: A rectangle has area $45\text{ cm}^2$ and perimeter $28\text{ cm}$. Find its whole-number dimensions.
development.solution_text:
$45=1\times45=3\times15=5\times9$
$2\times(5+9)=28$
The dimensions are $5\text{ cm}$ by $9\text{ cm}$.

mastery.question_text: A rectangle has area $96\text{ cm}^2$ and whole-number side lengths. Find its least possible perimeter and the dimensions that produce it.
mastery.solution_text:
$96=1\times96=2\times48=3\times32=4\times24=6\times16=8\times12$
The closest factor pair is $8$ and $12$.
$P=2\times(8+12)$
$=40\text{ cm}$

mastery.question_text: A rectangle has area $72\text{ m}^2$ and perimeter $36\text{ m}$. Find its whole-number dimensions.
mastery.solution_text:
$72=1\times72=2\times36=3\times24=4\times18=6\times12=8\times9$
$2\times(6+12)=36$
The dimensions are $6\text{ m}$ by $12\text{ m}$.

mastery.question_text: How many different rectangles with whole-number side lengths, area $120\text{ m}^2$ and perimeter at most $46\text{ m}$ are possible? Give their dimensions.
mastery.solution_text:
$120=1\times120=2\times60=3\times40=4\times30=5\times24=6\times20=8\times15=10\times12$
$P_{8\times15}=2\times23=46\text{ m}$
$P_{10\times12}=2\times22=44\text{ m}$
There are $2$ rectangles: $8\text{ m}\times15\text{ m}$ and $10\text{ m}\times12\text{ m}$.
